title: Where does the fire go?
hook: when a fire goes out, did it go north or south? the question doesn't fit

segments.voice: Yesterday: anupubba. Final knowledge comes by gradual training, from simply turning up to seeing for yourself. Which step did you take? Day four hundred sixty-three, a new week.

A birthday cake. Someone makes a wish and blows, and the little flames vanish, leaving thin gray ribbons of smoke. A five-year-old at the table asks: where did the fire go? Everyone laughs. But try answering. It didn't go to the kitchen. It didn't go up to the ceiling. The smoke did, but the smoke isn't the flame. A wanderer named Vacchagotta brings the Buddha a set of hard questions, the same ten from a few days ago, and the Buddha ends up asking him the five-year-old's question.
screen: `MAKE A WISH. BLOW.` → `WHERE DID THE FIRE GO?` → `VACCHAGOTTA'S QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Vacchagotta goes through the list. Is the world eternal? Is it not? Is the soul the same as the body? Does an awakened one exist after death? To each one, the Buddha says: I don't hold that view. Vacchagotta presses: do you have any view at all, then? The Buddha says he has put away views of that kind. What he has is seeing: how things arise and pass. Then Vacchagotta asks the hardest one: when a mind is fully freed, where does it reappear? Reappear doesn't apply, the Buddha says. Doesn't reappear? Doesn't apply. Both, neither? Doesn't apply. Vacchagotta is lost. I'm confused, he says. So the Buddha gives him the fire. If a fire were burning in front of you, would you know? Yes. And if someone asked what it was burning on? On grass and sticks. If it went out, would you know? Yes. Now, when it's out, which direction did it go: east, west, north or south? That doesn't apply, Vacchagotta says. It burned because of its fuel. When the fuel is used up and no more is added, it's simply counted as gone out. That's the answer. The question was built for things that travel. The word nibbāna, nirvana, draws on this very picture: going out, like a flame. The sutta doesn't say the freed one is annihilated, and it doesn't say they've gone somewhere else. It says they're deep and hard to measure, like the ocean. Buddhist schools have discussed this passage for centuries. The fire can't tell you north or south. The question doesn't fit.
screen: `I DON'T HOLD THAT VIEW.` · `REAPPEAR DOESN'T APPLY.` · `WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?` · `DEEP, LIKE THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: blow out a candle and ask. If you have a candle or a match nearby, and it's safe, light it and watch the flame for a few breaths. If not, picture one. Notice how it depends on the wick and the wax. Then blow it out, or picture it going out. Watch the smoke. Ask quietly: where did it go? Don't answer. Just sit with how the question doesn't fit. The bell holds the time.
nibbana. When a fire goes out, it didn't go north or south. It went out, because its fuel ran out. The Buddha's picture of nibbāna. Today's word.
Your line: the question doesn't fit. Today, when a question keeps going in circles, ask whether it's built for the thing you're asking about. Day four hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 463 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVEN THAT IS A VIEW.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across traditions use the image of a flame going out to explain nirvana, and many temples light candles and lamps on altars as a reminder of the teaching.

myth: in this sutta the Buddha says a freed one is annihilated at death
he says reappear, not reappear, both and neither all don't apply.
the word nibbāna draws on the image of a flame going out
the sutta's fire simile and the word share that picture.
Vacchagotta admits he's confused before the fire simile
he says he's lost; the fire is the Buddha's answer to that.

fork.setup: the fire in front of you has gone out. someone asks: did it go east, west, north or south? what do you say?
options: that doesn't apply: it went out when the fuel ran out
fork.reveal: Vacchagotta himself gives this answer, and the Buddha says the same holds for a fully freed one: the question doesn't fit.

original.note: Pali nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa): going out, like a flame whose fuel is spent.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana is a place you go.
what it means: a going out, like a fire when its fuel is gone; asking where it went doesn't fit.

what a scholar hears: MN 72, the Aggivacchagotta Sutta; the fire simile and the image of the freed one as 'deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom like the ocean' are central texts in debates about nirvana.
recall: a lion's roar: a bold claim

notes: MN 72 paraphrased; check the four 'does not apply' answers and the fire dialogue.
The ocean image (gambhīra, appameyya, duppariyogāha) is summarized as 'deep and hard to measure'; confirm.
The etymology of nibbāna as 'blowing out / going out' is standard but debated in its details; the script says the word 'draws on this very picture'; confirm.
